subject: Cloud Computing
title: Virtual Machines in Practice
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Virtual Machines in Practice.

hook.text: You request a server from AWS and it appears in 60 seconds. No human touched any hardware.

buildup.text: A virtual machine is a software-defined computer: you choose its CPU, memory, and storage size.

discovery.text: AWS calls them EC2 instances. Azure says Virtual Machines. Google uses Compute Engine. Same idea.

twist.text: VMs are flexible but wasteful. Most run at 10–20% capacity because users over-provision just in case.

climax.text: Despite newer options like containers, virtual machines still power most cloud workloads today.

punchline.text: Virtual machines: old technology, still the cloud's workhorse.

quiz.question: What is a common inefficiency with cloud virtual machines?
options: Users often over-provision, leaving most capacity unused
Virtual machines can only run one application at a time
They require manual rebooting every 24 hours

details.summary: Virtual machines in the cloud are provisioned in seconds, offer dozens of instance types optimized for different workloads, and can be started, stopped, resized, and terminated through APIs. Each VM provides an isolated environment with its own operating system and resources.
details.whyItMatters: VMs are the fundamental compute building block of cloud computing. Choosing the right instance type and understanding VM lifecycle management directly affects cost and performance.
takeaways: Cloud VMs provision in seconds with API-driven management
Instance types are optimized for compute, memory, or storage
Each VM runs an isolated operating system environment

faq.question: How do you choose the right instance type?
faq.answer: Match the instance type to your workload. Compute-optimized instances suit CPU-intensive tasks. Memory-optimized instances handle large databases. Storage-optimized instances are for data-intensive workloads. General-purpose instances balance all three for typical web applications.

faq.question: What happens when you stop a cloud VM?
faq.answer: When stopped, you stop paying for compute but retain attached storage. The VM's memory state is lost. When restarted, it may run on different physical hardware. Terminating a VM deletes it permanently, including ephemeral storage. Persistent storage volumes survive independently.
